news.headline: A New Baby Right Whale Gives Scientists Hope
news.body: Researchers found a baby North Atlantic right whale swimming with its mom near Quebec, Canada. That brings this season's count of new right whale calves to 24, the most since 2009. These whales are very rare, with only about 380 left, so every new baby is a big deal for the scientists who protect them.

news.headline: Astronomers Spot a Possible New Dwarf Planet
news.body: A telescope at the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile spotted a faraway object named 2026 ED138. It might be between 600 and 1,500 kilometres wide, which could make it one of the biggest dwarf planets ever found. Scientists need more data to be sure. If it is confirmed, it would become the sixth known dwarf planet, joining Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake and Ceres.

news.headline: Cuttlefish Check Their Work When They Hide
news.body: Cuttlefish can change their skin to look just like the sand and pebbles around them. A study found they do it in steps, pausing and adjusting to get closer to the seafloor pattern each time. It seems they check their own work as they go. Scientists still don't know exactly how the cuttlefish senses what its skin looks like.

fun_fact: A cuttlefish has three hearts and blue-green blood! 🦑
